newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: INTERVIEW-Dutch Enertel says phone demand booms.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Dutch Enertel says phone demand booms.

text.p: Dutch telecoms market debutant Enertel said on Friday demand for its services had way outstripped its expectations since its launch to customers earlier this week.
Enertel, an unlisted group of utilities and cable TV companies, made its first big pitch to customers on Tuesday following the July 1 liberalisation of Dutch voice telephony.

The group is offering a carrier selection option for international users, where callers dial into Enertel circuits from existing PTT lines, and is also offering leased lines and capacity for Internet service providers (ISPs).

"The carrier selection product is meeting very high demand, I can say after three or four days we're already meeting (the demand) we thought we would get for the whole of July," Enertel managing director Ad Ketelaars said in an interview.

He warned against over-optimism however, saying Enertel had yet to assess usage patterns. "You have to wait and see whether customers actually use the service to the degree that you want them to," he said.
"We're positively surprised by the demand. You always have your own expectations...this is significantly higher than we budgeted and that's good to see," he added.
Enertel is up against a welter of competition as new entrants hack away at the customer base of former fixed-line voice telephony monopolist Koninklijke PTT Nederland.

Among the competition is Telfort -- a partnership between British Telecom Plc and the Dutch national railway firm Nederlandse Spoorwegen -- and U.K.-headquartered independent telecoms service provider Esprit Telecom.

Ketelaars said he was expecting 1997 revenues of 200 million guilders from telecommunications. He stopped short of giving a specific forecast for 1998, but said he foresaw a solid rise in revenues as the new services kicked in.
He estimated around 150 million guilders of the 1997 revenues would come from internal business as the utilitity companies within the Enertel group continued to use existing networks.

"The internal isn't growing much. It's the external, the third-party business, where all the growth is coming from. The proportions will change. The total figure will rise a lot in 1998," Ketelaars said.

Ketelaars said Enertel's long-term strategy hinged on getting customers on to its own network and that the carrier selection option, to be followed up with offers for national calls next year, was a way of attracting customers.
"Ultimately, strategically the main thrust is with the cable. We're using the PTT as a way of getting customers. Through that we'll get a database of usage patterns," he said.
Enertel has around 6,000 km of optical fibre and sees that rising to 12,000 km over the next three years. Its cable TV operations cover 3.7 million Dutch households.

"Other carriers will come with carrier selection, but for us it's a means to an end, not an end in itself. The end in itself is to link customers to our own infrastructure, be it optical fibre or cable television," he said.
Ketelaars said its leased lines business was growing within its expectations, while its offerings for internet service providers was showing good potential.

"We provide ISPs with network for the customers to get to them, and we're also looking to link them to internet backbone in Holland. If you have bandwidth like we have, the internet is a good market for us."
